results.author: Joshua Gibson
highlights:
A week before the September jobs report, futures priced in about a 70% chance of a Federal Reserve (Fed) rate hike in October. After that, CME FedWatch, which turns futures prices into the odds of a Fed move, puts October at 21.59% and still prices in a December hike. The chance it gives a December hold is 0.00%.
...
FedWatch prices three more hikes by June 2027, which would take the Fed's rate to 4.50%-4.75%, and shows no chance of anything lower at the end of 2027. The highest of the 18 official projections for the end of 2027 is 4.375%, the middle of 4.25%-4.50%. President Logan said on Thursday that rates need to rise another half a percentage point or more.
...
FedWatch prices a second hike at 43.59% for January 27 and fully by March 17. With unemployment at 4.3% or lower, a payroll miss pushes that hike toward March and a payroll beat pulls it toward January. Unemployment at 4.4% or higher on either report is the condition that can move December, because it would break the range and the Fed's own projections at once.

Before either jobs report, the minutes of the September meeting arrive on October 7 and the September Consumer Price Index (CPI) on October 14. The lean is that the December hike holds, and that any drop in its odds on a payroll miss reverses while unemployment stays in range. The call is wrong if December's odds fall below 50% after a payroll miss with unemployment at 4.3% or lower. That would mean the jobs count itself had become a reason to stop.

The much softer-than-expected PCE inflation readings for August brought about some relief, removing the urgency for the Fed to hike again as soon as this month.

## Fed minutes may offer some direction

Most Fed officials see at least a further 25-bps hike by December according to the September dot plot, but the picture for 2027 is muddied. Although eight FOMC members predicted an additional hike next year, the rest either want to keep rates unchanged after the projected December increase or to cut them. The minutes of the September meeting due Wednesday might shed some light on whether the other 10 committee members could be convinced to join the hawkish camp if the inflation outlook doesn’t improve soon.

If the minutes strike a more hawkish tone than the post-meeting Fedspeak, the dollar is likely to extend its month-long winning streak, while stocks could face some selling pressure if yields surge again.

results.title: Week ahead – Fed minutes in the spotlight amid bond market rout

highlights:
Polymarket prices a 25-basis-point December hike at 75%. CME FedWatch places cumulative 25 bps at 67.8%, with an additional 18.8% probability of a cumulative 50-basis-point move — a meaningful tail. Three data points will drive December’s contract from here. The FOMC September minutes land Wednesday at 2 PM ET. Written before the jobs miss, they will reveal how broadly hawkish the committee’s baseline was in September and whether internal debate was already building. If the minutes show clean unanimity for continued tightening, December at 75% is defensible.
...
add context. With Kalshi pricing Democrats at 92% to win the House and 65% to win the Senate — and a full sweep favored at roughly 62–64% — the election will be decided before the Fed reconvenes in November. Whatever the political outcome, December is the first FOMC meeting since September 16 that carries no electoral proximity constraint. That is precisely why Polymarket has concentrated its rate-hike probability there, and why 75% is the number worth watching this week.

The October trade was always the wrong trade. Thirty-five years of institutional pattern, a 29,000-job payroll miss, and a vice chair’s public signal all pointed to the same conclusion. December at 75% on Polymarket is the live bet. Wednesday’s FOMC minutes are the first inflection point — they will tell traders whether the committee’s September hawkishness is durable enough to hold that contract through the data still ahead.

Goldman Sachs economists concluded, based on the Jefferson and Williams speeches, that October is off the table. The minutes will tell traders whether the committee reached that conclusion on September 16 or only after the data forced the issue.

The minutes are the appetizer. The main course arrives in sequence: September CPI on October 14, the FOMC decision October 27–28, September PCE on October 29, and the October jobs report on November 6 — all before December 8–9. Fed funds futures currently imply 3.3 hikes over the next twelve months, more aggressive than the median FOMC dot of one additional move. The gap between futures and the dot plot is the central tension in every rate-ladder trade right now.

For prediction market traders, the position is straightforward: watch the minutes Wednesday at 2 PM ET for how the committee framed neutral rate, energy risk, and the conditions for a pause. A hawkish record gives the hawks a benchmark to return to if October 14 delivers another inflation surprise. A neutral or dovish record makes the current patience look more settled — and December’s 71% a ceiling rather than a floor. The minutes won’t decide December. The CPI will. But the minutes will tell you which way the committee was already leaning before the data made the choice easier.
